instructional_moves.description: Teacher displays an image or primary source without context.
instructional_moves.say_script: Look at this image. Without any background, write down: What do you notice? What do you infer? What questions do you have?
instructional_moves.do_script: Project the image. Give students 2 minutes to write individually.

instructional_moves.description: Students record observations, inferences, and questions.
instructional_moves.say_script: Label three sections: Notice, Infer, Question. Be specific about what you see vs. what you guess.
instructional_moves.do_script: Students write. Teacher circulates and notes strong distinctions between observation and inference.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher leads a brief whole-class share to compare interpretations.
instructional_moves.say_script: Share one observation and one inference. Notice how different readers construct different meanings from the same image.
instructional_moves.do_script: Call on 3–4 students. Record a few observations and inferences on the board.

output_product: A three-section note (Notice, Infer, Question) with at least two specific observations and two inferences about the image or source.
contraindications: Do not use with images that are overly complex for a 5–7 minute warm-up.
Avoid images that require sensitive content protocols without safeguards in place.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher displays 2–3 headlines on the same event from different outlets.
instructional_moves.say_script: Compare these headlines about the same event. What words frame the story differently? Who is centered or marginalized?
instructional_moves.do_script: Project headlines. Give pairs 4 minutes to annotate differences.

instructional_moves.description: Pairs identify framing devices and implied audiences.
instructional_moves.say_script: Identify at least two word choices that shape meaning. Infer the intended audience for each headline.
instructional_moves.do_script: Pairs write on mini-whiteboards or paper. Teacher circulates and names strong observations.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher connects headline framing to the day's inquiry question.
instructional_moves.say_script: Today we'll ask: how do headlines construct 'truth' about power, and whose interests do they serve?
instructional_moves.do_script: Write the EQ and CIQ on the board, linking to headline analysis.

output_product: A pair-annotated comparison noting at least two framing word choices and an inferred audience for each headline.
contraindications: Do not use with highly polarizing current events unless sensitivity protocols are in place.
Limit to 2–3 headlines to keep the task focused.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher displays a single powerful image related to the unit theme.
instructional_moves.say_script: In your groups, analyze this image. Who is centered? Who is cropped out or in the background? What story does this tell about power?
instructional_moves.do_script: Project the image. Assign groups and display three prompts: Centered, Marginalized, Story about Power.

instructional_moves.description: Groups discuss and record answers to the three prompts.
instructional_moves.say_script: Use specific visual details: position, size, lighting, caption. Connect each detail to a claim about power.
instructional_moves.do_script: Groups write on a shared sheet or VNPS. Teacher circulates and pushes for evidence-based claims.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher names patterns and links to the day's inquiry.
instructional_moves.say_script: Notice how framing constructs meaning. Today we'll ask how this same logic shows up in our text.
instructional_moves.do_script: Record 2–3 strong group claims on the board and connect to the EQ.

output_product: A group analysis noting who is centered/marginalized in the image and one claim about how the image constructs power, supported by at least two visual details.
contraindications: Do not use images depicting graphic violence or trauma without sensitivity protocols.
Keep to one image to maintain focus in a short warm-up.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher introduces majoritarian story vs. counter-story.
instructional_moves.say_script: Today we'll start with a counter-story: a narrative that challenges a dominant or 'default' story about who matters, what counts as knowledge, or how power works.
instructional_moves.do_script: Display a brief definition and a 3–5 sentence counter-story excerpt or image caption.

instructional_moves.description: Students read/view the counter-story and respond to a focused prompt.
instructional_moves.say_script: Read this short counter-story silently. Then write for 3 minutes: What dominant story does this challenge? What evidence in the text supports that?
instructional_moves.do_script: Students write individually. Teacher monitors time and encourages specific textual reference.

instructional_moves.description: Students compare responses in pairs.
instructional_moves.say_script: Turn to a partner. Share your response. Together, identify one shared insight and one difference in how you read the counter-story.
instructional_moves.do_script: Pairs discuss for 2–3 minutes. Teacher listens in and notes strong comparisons to name aloud.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher connects the counter-story to the day's inquiry question and anchor text.
instructional_moves.say_script: Today, as we read our anchor text, we'll ask: whose story is centered, whose is marginalized, and how might counter-stories change our interpretation?
instructional_moves.do_script: Write the day's Essential Question and Critical Inquiry Question on the board, explicitly linking to the counter-story theme.

output_product: A 3–5 sentence quickwrite that identifies a dominant story challenged by the counter-story and cites at least one specific detail from the counter-story excerpt or image.
contraindications: Do not use if the counter-story excerpt is too long; keep it under 150 words or 1 short visual for a warm-up.
Avoid using counter-stories that require extensive background knowledge not yet built in the unit.
Do not use as a substitute for deeper counter-narrative work later in the unit; this is a hook, not the full analysis.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher poses a power-focused prompt tied to the day's text.
instructional_moves.say_script: Write for 4 minutes: Who has power in this excerpt? How is it gained, used, or resisted? Use at least one quote.
instructional_moves.do_script: Display the prompt and excerpt. Start a visible timer.

instructional_moves.description: Students write a focused response with textual evidence.
instructional_moves.say_script: Aim for 5–8 sentences. Make one clear claim and support it with at least one specific reference.
instructional_moves.do_script: Students write. Teacher circulates and notes strong claims to name later.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher uses 1–2 student claims to launch the day's inquiry.
instructional_moves.say_script: I heard strong claims about how power works here. Today we'll test and revise those claims as we read further.
instructional_moves.do_script: Read 1–2 anonymized student claims aloud and connect to the EQ.

output_product: A 5–8 sentence quickwrite making one claim about power in the excerpt, supported by at least one textual reference.
contraindications: Do not use when students have no prior exposure to the text and need more scaffolding.
Keep the prompt narrowly focused to fit a 6-minute warm-up.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher displays an image and asks what is missing.
instructional_moves.say_script: Look at this image. What or who is missing that you would expect? What story does that omission tell?
instructional_moves.do_script: Project the image. Give pairs 4 minutes to list omissions and inferences.

instructional_moves.description: Pairs list omissions and connect them to power or ideology.
instructional_moves.say_script: For each omission, ask: whose perspective is erased? What power dynamic does this serve?
instructional_moves.do_script: Pairs write on mini-whiteboards. Teacher circulates and pushes for systemic explanations.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher highlights how omissions construct meaning.
instructional_moves.say_script: Notice how what's left out shapes meaning as much as what's included. We'll look for similar silences in our text.
instructional_moves.do_script: Record 2–3 strong observations on the board and link to the CIQ.

output_product: A pair list of at least three omissions in the image, each connected to an inference about power or perspective.
contraindications: Do not use with images where omissions are too subtle for students' current skill level.
Avoid images that require sensitive content protocols without safeguards.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher displays 3–4 key academic or disciplinary words from the day's text.
instructional_moves.say_script: For each word, write: What do you think it means? What clues help you? Where have you seen it before?
instructional_moves.do_script: Project words in large font. Give students 3 minutes to write individually.

instructional_moves.description: Students compare definitions and refine using context clues.
instructional_moves.say_script: Compare your definitions. Agree on a shared, student-friendly definition for each word.
instructional_moves.do_script: Pairs write shared definitions. Teacher circulates and corrects major misconceptions.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher confirms accurate definitions and links to the text.
instructional_moves.say_script: These words will help us track how the author constructs power and meaning today.
instructional_moves.do_script: Display correct definitions briefly and refer back during reading.

output_product: A set of 3–4 student-friendly definitions co-constructed in pairs, each tied to a word from the day's text.
contraindications: Do not use for more than 4 words in a short warm-up.
Avoid highly abstract terms without concrete context in the day's excerpt.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher displays a short excerpt (2–4 sentences) from a speech or article.
instructional_moves.say_script: Identify one rhetorical move (e.g., appeal to emotion, logic, credibility). How does it try to persuade the audience?
instructional_moves.do_script: Project the excerpt. Give students 3 minutes to annotate.

instructional_moves.description: Students label the rhetorical move and explain its effect.
instructional_moves.say_script: Write 2–3 sentences: name the move, cite the phrase, explain the intended effect.
instructional_moves.do_script: Students write. Teacher scans for strong examples.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher names patterns and links to the day's inquiry.
instructional_moves.say_script: We're seeing how language constructs audiences and positions readers. Today we'll track this across the full text.
instructional_moves.do_script: Read 1–2 strong student examples aloud and connect to the EQ.

output_product: A 2–3 sentence annotation identifying one rhetorical move, citing the phrase, and explaining its intended effect.
contraindications: Do not use with excerpts that are too long or linguistically dense for a 7-minute warm-up.
Ensure students have prior exposure to basic rhetorical appeals.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher displays a short quote from a dominant character or authority.
instructional_moves.say_script: Rewrite this quote from the perspective of a marginalized or silent character. How does the meaning change?
instructional_moves.do_script: Project the quote. Assign pairs and display the task.

instructional_moves.description: Pairs rewrite the quote and note how meaning shifts.
instructional_moves.say_script: Write 2–4 sentences in the new voice. Then note: what changes about power, knowledge, or legitimacy?
instructional_moves.do_script: Pairs write on mini-whiteboards. Teacher circulates and names strong perspective shifts.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher connects perspective shifts to the day's inquiry.
instructional_moves.say_script: Today we'll ask: whose voice counts as knowledge, and how might centering other voices change our interpretation?
instructional_moves.do_script: Read 1–2 rewrites aloud and link to the CIQ.

output_product: A 2–4 sentence rewritten quote from a marginalized or silent perspective, plus 1–2 sentences noting how power or meaning changes.
contraindications: Do not use when students lack basic understanding of the characters or context.
Avoid quotes tied to highly sensitive topics without safeguards.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher sets a short timed reading sprint (1–2 paragraphs).
instructional_moves.say_script: Read this excerpt silently for 3 minutes. Mark anything that surprises, confuses, or connects to our unit question.
instructional_moves.do_script: Display the excerpt and start a visible timer.

instructional_moves.description: Students read and annotate for surprise/confusion/connection.
instructional_moves.say_script: Use symbols: ! for surprise, ? for confusion, * for connection. Aim for at least two marks.
instructional_moves.do_script: Students read and annotate. Teacher monitors pacing.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher uses annotations to launch the day's inquiry.
instructional_moves.say_script: We'll start with your questions and connections. These will drive our investigation today.
instructional_moves.do_script: Collect 2–3 student questions and write them on the board.

output_product: An annotated excerpt with at least two marks (surprise, confusion, or connection) tied to the unit question.
contraindications: Do not use with excerpts that are too long for a 6-minute sprint.
Ensure the excerpt is accessible enough for independent reading.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher names and defines the critical lens in accessible language.
instructional_moves.say_script: Today we'll use a [lens] lens. This means we'll ask: [2–3 guiding questions].
instructional_moves.do_script: Display the lens name, a simple definition, and 2–3 guiding questions.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher models applying the lens to a short excerpt.
instructional_moves.say_script: Watch how I apply this lens. I notice ______, which suggests ______ about power/identity/representation.
instructional_moves.do_script: Annotate the excerpt on the board, highlighting evidence tied to the lens questions.

instructional_moves.description: Students apply the lens to a new excerpt in pairs.
instructional_moves.say_script: In pairs, find one piece of evidence that this lens helps explain. Write one claim using our language frame.
instructional_moves.do_script: Pairs write on mini-whiteboards. Teacher circulates and names strong lens-based claims.

output_product: A pair-generated claim that applies the critical lens to a specific piece of textual or visual evidence.
contraindications: Do not introduce more than one new lens in a single lesson.
Avoid highly abstract lenses without concrete examples.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher defines 'ideological framing' in accessible language.
instructional_moves.say_script: Ideological framing is how language and images position certain ideas as normal or natural. We'll look for words and images that do this.
instructional_moves.do_script: Display a simple definition and 2 examples from familiar contexts.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher models identifying framing in a short text.
instructional_moves.say_script: Notice how this phrase positions ______ as normal. What alternative framing is left out?
instructional_moves.do_script: Annotate 2–3 key phrases on the board, naming the implied ideology.

instructional_moves.description: Students identify one framing move in a new excerpt.
instructional_moves.say_script: Find one phrase that frames an idea as normal. Write: What ideology is implied? What alternative is silenced?
instructional_moves.do_script: Students write individually or in pairs. Teacher collects examples to discuss.

output_product: A written analysis identifying one ideological framing move, the implied ideology, and one silenced alternative.
contraindications: Do not use with texts where ideological framing is too subtle for students' current level.
Ensure students have prior practice with basic framing concepts.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher presents 2–3 key historical facts relevant to the text.
instructional_moves.say_script: These three facts will help us read this text in context. As we read, ask: how does this change our interpretation?
instructional_moves.do_script: Display bullet-pointed historical context with dates and actors.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher models connecting one historical fact to a passage.
instructional_moves.say_script: Knowing that ______, this line now suggests ______. Before, I might have read it as ______.
instructional_moves.do_script: Annotate a short passage on the board, linking to one historical fact.

instructional_moves.description: Students connect a different historical fact to a new passage.
instructional_moves.say_script: In pairs, choose one historical fact and one passage. Write: How does this context change the meaning?
instructional_moves.do_script: Pairs write on mini-whiteboards. Teacher circulates and names strong connections.

output_product: A pair-written connection between one historical fact and one passage, explaining how context shifts meaning.
contraindications: Do not overload with more than 3 historical facts in a short mini-lesson.
Ensure historical facts are accurate and sourced.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher defines subtext and silence as analytical categories.
instructional_moves.say_script: Subtext is what's implied but not said. Silence is what's left out entirely. We'll track both.
instructional_moves.do_script: Display definitions and 1–2 examples from familiar texts.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher models identifying subtext and silence in a short scene or passage.
instructional_moves.say_script: Here, the character says ______, but their action suggests ______. Also notice who is not speaking at all.
instructional_moves.do_script: Annotate a short excerpt, marking subtext and silences.

instructional_moves.description: Students identify one subtext and one silence in a new excerpt.
instructional_moves.say_script: Find one moment of subtext and one silence. Write: What power dynamic does each reveal?
instructional_moves.do_script: Students write individually or in pairs. Teacher collects examples for discussion.

output_product: A written analysis identifying one moment of subtext and one silence, each connected to a power dynamic.
contraindications: Do not use with texts where subtext is too opaque for students' current skill level.
Ensure students have prior practice with inference and implication.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher assigns groups and displays a simple power diagram template.
instructional_moves.say_script: Map the power relationships in this scene. Use arrows to show who influences whom and how.
instructional_moves.do_script: Project a template with characters/nodes and example arrows labeled 'coerces', 'persuades', 'resists'.

instructional_moves.description: Groups create a power map for the assigned scene or chapter.
instructional_moves.say_script: Include at least four characters or groups. Label each arrow with a specific tactic or mechanism of power.
instructional_moves.do_script: Groups draw on VNPS or large paper. Teacher circulates and pushes for specificity.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher leads a brief gallery walk and names patterns.
instructional_moves.say_script: Notice where power is centralized, where it's resisted, and where it's invisible.
instructional_moves.do_script: Students walk and observe. Teacher highlights 2–3 strong diagrams.

output_product: A group-created power dynamics diagram with at least four nodes and labeled arrows showing mechanisms of power.
contraindications: Do not use with very short excerpts that lack multiple actors.
Ensure students understand basic power vocabulary (coerce, persuade, resist, etc.).

instructional_moves.description: Teacher introduces a simplified discourse analysis framework (e.g., who can speak, what can be said, what counts as truth).
instructional_moves.say_script: We'll ask: Who is allowed to speak? What topics are allowed? What counts as 'truth' here?
instructional_moves.do_script: Display the three questions and a short example from a familiar text.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher models applying the framework to a short policy or speech excerpt.
instructional_moves.say_script: In this passage, only ______ can speak authoritatively. Topics like ______ are treated as off-limits.
instructional_moves.do_script: Annotate the excerpt, marking who speaks, what is sayable, and what is validated as truth.

instructional_moves.description: Students apply the framework to a new excerpt in pairs.
instructional_moves.say_script: Use the three questions to analyze this passage. Write one claim about how discourse constructs power.
instructional_moves.do_script: Pairs write on mini-whiteboards. Teacher circulates and names strong discourse-based claims.

output_product: A pair-written claim about how discourse constructs power in the excerpt, supported by at least two textual references.
contraindications: Do not use with texts that lack clear discursive rules or authority structures.
Ensure students have prior exposure to basic discourse concepts.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher assigns groups and defines 'institutional narrative'.
instructional_moves.say_script: An institutional narrative is the story an organization tells about itself. Map how this institution constructs its identity and authority.
instructional_moves.do_script: Display a simple template: Mission, Authority, Beneficiaries, Silences.

instructional_moves.description: Groups analyze a policy, report, or institutional text and fill the template.
instructional_moves.say_script: For each section, cite specific phrases or sections from the text.
instructional_moves.do_script: Groups write on VNPS or large paper. Teacher circulates and pushes for textual evidence.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher leads a brief share-out and names patterns across groups.
instructional_moves.say_script: Notice whose interests are centered, whose are marginalized, and what is left unsaid.
instructional_moves.do_script: Record key observations on the board and link to the unit EQ.

output_product: A group-created institutional narrative map with four sections (Mission, Authority, Beneficiaries, Silences), each supported by textual evidence.
contraindications: Do not use with very short texts that lack institutional language.
Ensure students can distinguish between stated mission and actual effects.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher defines counter-narrative and contrasts it with dominant narratives.
instructional_moves.say_script: A counter-narrative challenges a dominant story about who matters and what counts as knowledge.
instructional_moves.do_script: Display a simple definition and 1–2 examples from familiar contexts.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher models identifying counter-narrative moves in a short text.
instructional_moves.say_script: Notice how this passage centers a voice usually marginalized. It reframes ______ as ______.
instructional_moves.do_script: Annotate a short excerpt, marking counter-narrative moves.

instructional_moves.description: Students identify one counter-narrative move in a new excerpt.
instructional_moves.say_script: Find one passage that challenges a dominant story. Write: What story is challenged? How?
instructional_moves.do_script: Students write individually or in pairs. Teacher collects examples for discussion.

output_product: A written analysis identifying one counter-narrative move, the dominant story it challenges, and how it reframes meaning.
contraindications: Do not use with texts where counter-narrative is too implicit for students' current level.
Ensure students have prior exposure to dominant vs. counter-narrative concepts.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher explains that they will model their thinking while reading.
instructional_moves.say_script: I'll read this passage aloud and share my thinking as I go. Notice how I question, infer, and connect.
instructional_moves.do_script: Display the excerpt and begin reading with pauses for thinking aloud.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher models critical questions and inferences while reading.
instructional_moves.say_script: I notice ______. This makes me wonder ______. This positions the reader to ______.
instructional_moves.do_script: Annotate thinking on the board in real time.

instructional_moves.description: Students practice think-aloud in pairs with a new excerpt.
instructional_moves.say_script: Take turns reading and thinking aloud. Use: I notice, I infer, This positions the reader to.
instructional_moves.do_script: Pairs read and annotate. Teacher circulates and names strong moves.

output_product: A pair-annotated excerpt with at least three think-aloud moves (notice, infer, position).
contraindications: Do not use with texts that are too dense for real-time thinking aloud.
Ensure students have prior exposure to think-aloud protocols.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher explains the margins-to-center protocol.
instructional_moves.say_script: We'll annotate by asking: Who is in the margins? How might centering them change our reading?
instructional_moves.do_script: Display a simple annotation key: M = marginal voice, C = central voice, ? = question.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher models annotating a short passage with M/C/? marks.
instructional_moves.say_script: Here, ______ is in the margin. If we center their perspective, the story shifts to ______.
instructional_moves.do_script: Annotate a short excerpt on the board, marking M/C/?.

instructional_moves.description: Students annotate a new passage using the same protocol.
instructional_moves.say_script: Mark at least two marginal voices and one central voice. Write one claim about how centering a marginal voice changes meaning.
instructional_moves.do_script: Students annotate individually or in pairs. Teacher circulates and names strong shifts.

output_product: An annotated passage with at least two marginal voices, one central voice, and one claim about how centering a marginal voice changes meaning.
contraindications: Do not use with texts that lack clear marginal/central distinctions.
Ensure students understand the difference between marginal and central voices.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher defines rhetorical stance (author, audience, purpose, context).
instructional_moves.say_script: We'll analyze how the author's stance shapes meaning. Ask: Who is the author? Who is the audience? What is the purpose? What is the context?
instructional_moves.do_script: Display the four questions and a short example.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher models analyzing stance in a short speech or essay excerpt.
instructional_moves.say_script: Given this audience and purpose, the author chooses ______. This positions the reader to ______.
instructional_moves.do_script: Annotate the excerpt, linking stance choices to effects.

instructional_moves.description: Students analyze stance in a new excerpt in pairs.
instructional_moves.say_script: Use the four questions to analyze this passage. Write one claim about how stance constructs power.
instructional_moves.do_script: Pairs write on mini-whiteboards. Teacher circulates and names strong stance-based claims.

output_product: A pair-written claim about how rhetorical stance constructs power in the excerpt, supported by at least two textual references.
contraindications: Do not use with texts where author/audience/purpose are unclear.
Ensure students have prior exposure to basic rhetorical concepts.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher introduces problem-posing reading as asking critical questions while reading.
instructional_moves.say_script: We'll read by asking: What problem is this text responding to? Who benefits? Who is harmed?
instructional_moves.do_script: Display the three questions and a short example.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher models problem-posing questions on a short excerpt.
instructional_moves.say_script: This passage seems to respond to ______. It benefits ______ and potentially harms ______.
instructional_moves.do_script: Annotate the excerpt with problem-posing questions and tentative answers.

instructional_moves.description: Students apply problem-posing questions to a new excerpt in pairs.
instructional_moves.say_script: Use the three questions to analyze this passage. Write one claim about the problem and its stakes.
instructional_moves.do_script: Pairs write on mini-whiteboards. Teacher circulates and names strong problem-posing claims.

output_product: A pair-written claim identifying the problem the text responds to, who benefits, and who is harmed, supported by textual evidence.
contraindications: Do not use with texts that lack clear social or political stakes.
Ensure students have prior exposure to problem-posing concepts.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher introduces two texts that speak to each other (e.g., canonical + counter-text).
instructional_moves.say_script: We'll read these two texts together. Ask: How does each construct power, identity, or knowledge differently?
instructional_moves.do_script: Display both excerpts side by side.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher models one point of comparison.
instructional_moves.say_script: In Text A, ______ is centered. In Text B, ______ is centered. This shifts the story from ______ to ______.
instructional_moves.do_script: Annotate both excerpts, highlighting one key contrast.

instructional_moves.description: Students identify one additional point of comparison in pairs.
instructional_moves.say_script: Find one more contrast. Write: How does this change your interpretation of power or knowledge?
instructional_moves.do_script: Pairs write on mini-whiteboards. Teacher circulates and names strong comparisons.

output_product: A pair-written comparison identifying one additional contrast between the two texts and explaining how it changes interpretation of power or knowledge.
contraindications: Do not use with texts that are too long or complex for side-by-side analysis in one lesson.
Ensure students have prior exposure to both texts.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher defines stereotype and explains how texts reproduce or challenge them.
instructional_moves.say_script: A stereotype is an oversimplified idea about a group. We'll look for where this text reproduces or challenges stereotypes.
instructional_moves.do_script: Display a simple definition and 1–2 examples.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher models identifying a stereotype in a short excerpt or scene.
instructional_moves.say_script: This character is described as ______, which echoes a stereotype about ______. Notice what is left out.
instructional_moves.do_script: Annotate the excerpt or describe the scene, marking stereotypical language or imagery.

instructional_moves.description: Students identify one stereotype in a new excerpt or scene.
instructional_moves.say_script: Find one stereotype. Write: What group is stereotyped? How? What alternative is silenced?
instructional_moves.do_script: Students write individually or in pairs. Teacher collects examples for discussion.

output_product: A written analysis identifying one stereotype, the group stereotyped, how it is constructed, and one silenced alternative.
contraindications: Do not use with texts where stereotypes are too subtle for students' current level.
Ensure a safe classroom culture for discussing stereotypes.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher divides the class into expert groups, each with a different counter-perspective text.
instructional_moves.say_script: Each group will become experts on one counter-perspective text. Ask: What dominant story does this challenge? What evidence supports that?
instructional_moves.do_script: Assign texts and groups. Display guiding questions.

instructional_moves.description: Expert groups read and analyze their counter-perspective text.
instructional_moves.say_script: Prepare to teach your text to a new group. Identify one key claim and two pieces of evidence.
instructional_moves.do_script: Groups annotate and prepare a brief teaching outline.

instructional_moves.description: Students regroup so each new group has one expert per text.
instructional_moves.say_script: Teach your text to your new group. Then compare: how do these counter-perspectives intersect or differ?
instructional_moves.do_script: Students teach and discuss. Teacher circulates and names strong connections.

output_product: A group comparison noting how multiple counter-perspectives intersect or differ in challenging dominant stories.
contraindications: Do not use with too many texts; limit to 3–4 counter-perspectives.
Ensure all texts are accessible enough for expert-group analysis.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher sets up an inner circle (debate) and outer circle (observers).
instructional_moves.say_script: Inner circle will debate: [debatable question]. Outer circle will track argument moves and evidence.
instructional_moves.do_script: Arrange chairs in two concentric circles. Display the debate question and observer roles.

instructional_moves.description: Inner circle debates; outer circle observes and records.
instructional_moves.say_script: Debate using textual evidence. Observers: note claims, evidence, and counterclaims.
instructional_moves.do_script: Students debate for 15–20 minutes. Observers take notes.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher leads a debrief connecting debate to the unit inquiry.
instructional_moves.say_script: What claims were strongest? Where did evidence change the argument? How does this connect to our EQ?
instructional_moves.do_script: Facilitate a whole-class reflection. Record key insights on the board.

output_product: Observer notes tracking claims, evidence, and counterclaims, plus a whole-class reflection connecting the debate to the unit EQ.
contraindications: Do not use with highly sensitive topics without established norms and safeguards.
Ensure students have prior practice with evidence-based discussion.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher forms visibly random groups of 3 and assigns each a vertical board.
instructional_moves.say_script: In your groups, analyze this prompt on the board. Use evidence from the text to support your claims.
instructional_moves.do_script: Display the prompt and excerpt. Assign groups to boards.

instructional_moves.description: Groups write their analysis on the vertical board.
instructional_moves.say_script: Write your claim, evidence, and reasoning. Make it visible and clear for others to read.
instructional_moves.do_script: Groups write on VNPS. Teacher circulates and pushes for evidence-based claims.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher leads a gallery walk and names strong moves.
instructional_moves.say_script: Notice where groups use evidence differently. Where do you see claim revision?
instructional_moves.do_script: Students walk and observe. Teacher highlights 2–3 strong boards.

output_product: A group-written vertical board analysis with a clear claim, textual evidence, and reasoning.
contraindications: Do not use if vertical surfaces are unavailable.
Keep groups to 3–4 students to ensure individual accountability.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher posts multiple texts, images, or student artifacts around the room.
instructional_moves.say_script: In your groups, rotate to each station. At each, write one observation and one question.
instructional_moves.do_script: Post artifacts with space for writing. Assign starting stations.

instructional_moves.description: Groups rotate and annotate each station.
instructional_moves.say_script: Spend 3 minutes per station. Write clearly so others can read.
instructional_moves.do_script: Groups rotate and write. Teacher monitors pacing.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher leads a debrief connecting observations to the unit inquiry.
instructional_moves.say_script: What patterns do you see across stations? How does this connect to our EQ?
instructional_moves.do_script: Facilitate a whole-class discussion. Record key insights on the board.

output_product: Annotated stations with observations and questions from each group, plus a whole-class synthesis.
contraindications: Do not use with too many stations; limit to 4–6 for a 25-minute activity.
Ensure all artifacts are accessible enough for quick analysis.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher arranges a Socratic circle and introduces the critical lens focus.
instructional_moves.say_script: Today's seminar question is: [open-ended question]. We'll use a [lens] lens to guide our discussion.
instructional_moves.do_script: Display the seminar question and lens guiding questions.

instructional_moves.description: Students discuss the text using the lens and seminar norms.
instructional_moves.say_script: Use textual evidence. Build on others' ideas. Challenge respectfully.
instructional_moves.do_script: Students discuss. Teacher facilitates and takes notes on argument moves.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher leads a reflection on discussion quality and insights.
instructional_moves.say_script: What claims shifted during the discussion? Where did evidence change the argument?
instructional_moves.do_script: Facilitate a brief reflection. Record key insights on the board.

output_product: A whole-class discussion with tracked argument moves and a reflection on claim shifts.
contraindications: Do not use with texts that are too short or lack complexity for sustained discussion.
Ensure students have prior practice with Socratic norms.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher introduces the dialectical journal format (quotes + responses).
instructional_moves.say_script: On the left, write significant quotes. On the right, write your responses: questions, connections, critiques.
instructional_moves.do_script: Display a sample journal entry.

instructional_moves.description: Pairs read and create dialectical journal entries.
instructional_moves.say_script: Aim for at least three quotes with responses. Use our critical lens questions to guide your responses.
instructional_moves.do_script: Pairs read and write. Teacher circulates and names strong entries.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher leads a brief share-out of strong journal entries.
instructional_moves.say_script: Share one quote and response that shifted your thinking.
instructional_moves.do_script: Call on 2–3 pairs to share. Record key insights on the board.

output_product: A dialectical journal with at least three quotes and critical responses.
contraindications: Do not use with texts that are too short for multiple significant quotes.
Ensure students understand the difference between summary and critical response.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher assigns roles based on characters or historical figures from the text.
instructional_moves.say_script: In your groups, each person will take on a role. Speak from that perspective in the scenario.
instructional_moves.do_script: Distribute role cards with brief descriptions and goals.

instructional_moves.description: Groups enact a scenario or conversation from their assigned perspectives.
instructional_moves.say_script: Stay in character. Use evidence from the text to support your perspective's goals.
instructional_moves.do_script: Groups roleplay for 10–15 minutes. Teacher circulates and notes strong perspective-taking.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher leads a debrief connecting roleplay to the unit inquiry.
instructional_moves.say_script: How did different perspectives conflict or align? What does this reveal about power?
instructional_moves.do_script: Facilitate a whole-class discussion. Record key insights on the board.

output_product: A group roleplay and whole-class debrief noting how different perspectives reveal power dynamics.
contraindications: Do not use with highly sensitive topics without established norms and safeguards.
Ensure all roles are clearly defined and respectful.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher introduces mind mapping as a way to visualize structural power.
instructional_moves.say_script: Create a mind map showing how power flows in this text. Include institutions, groups, and mechanisms.
instructional_moves.do_script: Display a simple example mind map.

instructional_moves.description: Groups create a mind map of structural power in the text.
instructional_moves.say_script: Use nodes for actors and institutions. Label connections with mechanisms of power (e.g., law, economy, ideology).
instructional_moves.do_script: Groups draw on VNPS or large paper. Teacher circulates and pushes for specificity.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher leads a gallery walk and names patterns.
instructional_moves.say_script: Notice where power is centralized, where it's resisted, and where it's invisible.
instructional_moves.do_script: Students walk and observe. Teacher highlights 2–3 strong maps.

output_product: A group-created mind map showing structural power relationships, with labeled nodes and mechanisms.
contraindications: Do not use with texts that lack clear structural power dynamics.
Ensure students have prior exposure to basic power vocabulary.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher introduces the counter-narrative writing task.
instructional_moves.say_script: Write a short counter-narrative that challenges a dominant story from our text. Center a marginalized voice.
instructional_moves.do_script: Display the task and success criteria.

instructional_moves.description: Students draft their counter-narrative.
instructional_moves.say_script: Aim for 1–2 pages. Use specific details and dialogue. Show how this perspective changes the story.
instructional_moves.do_script: Students write. Teacher conferences with individuals as needed.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher provides formative feedback on drafts.
instructional_moves.say_script: I'll confer with each of you. Focus on how clearly your counter-narrative challenges the dominant story.
instructional_moves.do_script: Teacher holds brief conferences. Students revise as time allows.

output_product: A 1–2 page counter-narrative draft centering a marginalized voice and challenging a dominant story.
contraindications: Do not use without prior analysis of dominant and counter-narratives.
Ensure students have access to writing supports (frames, examples).

instructional_moves.description: Teacher introduces the rhetorical analysis essay task.
instructional_moves.say_script: Draft an essay analyzing how the author uses rhetorical strategies to construct power and meaning.
instructional_moves.do_script: Display the prompt and rubric.

instructional_moves.description: Students draft their rhetorical analysis essay.
instructional_moves.say_script: Include a clear thesis, textual evidence, and analysis of rhetorical strategies.
instructional_moves.do_script: Students write. Teacher conferences with individuals as needed.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher provides formative feedback on drafts.
instructional_moves.say_script: I'll confer with each of you. Focus on how clearly your analysis connects rhetoric to power.
instructional_moves.do_script: Teacher holds brief conferences. Students revise as time allows.

output_product: A rhetorical analysis essay draft with a clear thesis, textual evidence, and analysis of rhetorical strategies.
contraindications: Do not use without prior instruction on rhetorical analysis.
Ensure students have access to writing supports (outlines, examples).

instructional_moves.description: Teacher introduces the investigative dossier task.
instructional_moves.say_script: Compile a dossier of 3–5 texts that investigate our unit question from different angles.
instructional_moves.do_script: Display the task and success criteria.

instructional_moves.description: Students select and annotate texts for their dossier.
instructional_moves.say_script: For each text, write a brief annotation: source, claim, evidence, and how it connects to our inquiry.
instructional_moves.do_script: Students research and annotate. Teacher confers as needed.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher provides formative feedback on dossiers.
instructional_moves.say_script: I'll review your dossiers. Focus on how well your texts triangulate the inquiry question.
instructional_moves.do_script: Teacher reviews and provides written or verbal feedback.

output_product: An investigative dossier of 3–5 annotated texts triangulating the unit inquiry question.
contraindications: Do not use without prior instruction on source evaluation.
Ensure students have access to research tools and databases.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher introduces the voice amplification task.
instructional_moves.say_script: Rewrite a scene or passage from the perspective of a marginalized or silent character.
instructional_moves.do_script: Display the task and success criteria.

instructional_moves.description: Students draft their voice amplification rewrite.
instructional_moves.say_script: Aim for 1–2 pages. Use specific details and dialogue. Show how this perspective changes the story.
instructional_moves.do_script: Students write. Teacher conferences with individuals as needed.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher provides formative feedback on drafts.
instructional_moves.say_script: I'll confer with each of you. Focus on how clearly your rewrite amplifies a silenced voice.
instructional_moves.do_script: Teacher holds brief conferences. Students revise as time allows.

output_product: A 1–2 page rewrite of a scene or passage from a marginalized or silent character's perspective.
contraindications: Do not use without prior analysis of marginal and central voices.
Ensure students have access to writing supports (frames, examples).

instructional_moves.description: Teacher introduces the media framing matrix task.
instructional_moves.say_script: Create a matrix comparing how different outlets frame the same event.
instructional_moves.do_script: Display a sample matrix with outlets as rows and framing elements as columns.

instructional_moves.description: Students select 2–3 outlets and complete the matrix.
instructional_moves.say_script: For each outlet, note headline, word choice, images, and implied audience.
instructional_moves.do_script: Students work individually. Teacher circulates and names strong comparisons.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher leads a brief share-out of matrix findings.
instructional_moves.say_script: Share one pattern you noticed. How does framing construct different 'truths'?
instructional_moves.do_script: Call on 2–3 students to share. Record key insights on the board.

output_product: A media framing contrast matrix comparing 2–3 outlets' coverage of the same event.
contraindications: Do not use with highly polarizing current events without sensitivity protocols.
Ensure students have access to multiple news sources.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher introduces the primary source synthesis task.
instructional_moves.say_script: Synthesize 2–3 primary sources to construct an evidence-based claim about our inquiry question.
instructional_moves.do_script: Display the task and success criteria.

instructional_moves.description: Students analyze and synthesize primary sources.
instructional_moves.say_script: Write a 1–2 paragraph synthesis. Use direct quotes and explain how they support your claim.
instructional_moves.do_script: Students write. Teacher confers as needed.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher provides formative feedback on syntheses.
instructional_moves.say_script: I'll review your syntheses. Focus on how well you integrate evidence from multiple sources.
instructional_moves.do_script: Teacher reviews and provides written or verbal feedback.

output_product: A 1–2 paragraph synthesis of 2–3 primary sources constructing an evidence-based claim.
contraindications: Do not use with sources that are too complex for independent analysis.
Ensure students have prior instruction on source synthesis.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher displays the exit ticket prompt.
instructional_moves.say_script: Answer this question before you leave: [critical question tied to the day's inquiry].
instructional_moves.do_script: Project the prompt. Distribute slips or digital form.

instructional_moves.description: Students write their exit ticket response.
instructional_moves.say_script: Be specific. Use at least one reference to today's text or discussion.
instructional_moves.do_script: Students write. Teacher collects responses.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher reviews exit tickets to inform the next lesson.
instructional_moves.say_script: I'll read these to plan our next steps. Notice any patterns or misconceptions.
instructional_moves.do_script: Teacher reviews and notes common themes.

output_product: An individual exit ticket response to a critical question tied to the day's inquiry.
contraindications: Do not use with overly broad prompts; keep the question focused.
Ensure the prompt is accessible to all students.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher introduces the assumptions audit prompt.
instructional_moves.say_script: Reflect: What assumption did you enter today with? What evidence challenged or confirmed it?
instructional_moves.do_script: Display the prompt. Distribute slips or digital form.

instructional_moves.description: Students write their assumptions audit.
instructional_moves.say_script: Be specific. Name the assumption and the evidence that shifted your thinking.
instructional_moves.do_script: Students write. Teacher collects responses.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher reviews audits to track claim revision.
instructional_moves.say_script: I'll read these to see how your thinking evolved. Notice any patterns.
instructional_moves.do_script: Teacher reviews and notes common themes.

output_product: An individual reflection naming one assumption and the evidence that challenged or confirmed it.
contraindications: Do not use without prior modeling of assumption-tracking.
Ensure the prompt is accessible to all students.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher introduces the synthesis statement prompt.
instructional_moves.say_script: Write one sentence that synthesizes today's learning: 'Today I learned that ______.'
instructional_moves.do_script: Display the prompt. Distribute slips or digital form.

instructional_moves.description: Students write their synthesis statement.
instructional_moves.say_script: Be specific. Connect to our unit question.
instructional_moves.do_script: Students write. Teacher collects responses.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher reviews statements to assess understanding.
instructional_moves.say_script: I'll read these to see what stuck. Notice any patterns.
instructional_moves.do_script: Teacher reviews and notes common themes.

output_product: An individual one-sentence synthesis of today's learning connected to the unit question.
contraindications: Do not use with overly broad prompts; keep the question focused.
Ensure the prompt is accessible to all students.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher introduces the equity voice assessment prompt.
instructional_moves.say_script: Reflect: Whose voice was centered today? Whose was marginalized? How did this affect our discussion?
instructional_moves.do_script: Display the prompt. Distribute slips or digital form.

instructional_moves.description: Students write their equity voice assessment.
instructional_moves.say_script: Be specific. Name at least one voice and one effect.
instructional_moves.do_script: Students write. Teacher collects responses.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher reviews assessments to track equity patterns.
instructional_moves.say_script: I'll read these to see whose voices we centered or marginalized. Notice any patterns.
instructional_moves.do_script: Teacher reviews and notes common themes.

output_product: An individual reflection naming whose voice was centered/marginalized and how this affected discussion.
contraindications: Do not use without prior modeling of equity-focused reflection.
Ensure the prompt is accessible to all students.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher introduces the counter-perspective check prompt.
instructional_moves.say_script: What counter-perspective did we consider today? How did it change your interpretation?
instructional_moves.do_script: Display the prompt. Distribute slips or digital form.

instructional_moves.description: Students write their counter-perspective check.
instructional_moves.say_script: Be specific. Name the perspective and the shift in your thinking.
instructional_moves.do_script: Students write. Teacher collects responses.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher reviews checks to track perspective-taking.
instructional_moves.say_script: I'll read these to see how counter-perspectives shifted thinking. Notice any patterns.
instructional_moves.do_script: Teacher reviews and notes common themes.

output_product: An individual reflection naming one counter-perspective and how it changed interpretation.
contraindications: Do not use without prior analysis of counter-perspectives.
Ensure the prompt is accessible to all students.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher introduces the metacognitive pedagogy log prompt.
instructional_moves.say_script: Reflect: What teaching moves helped you think critically today? How can you use these moves in your own learning?
instructional_moves.do_script: Display the prompt. Distribute slips or digital form.

instructional_moves.description: Students write their metacognitive pedagogy log.
instructional_moves.say_script: Be specific. Name at least one teaching move and one application.
instructional_moves.do_script: Students write. Teacher collects responses.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher reviews logs to refine pedagogy.
instructional_moves.say_script: I'll read these to see what worked. Notice any patterns.
instructional_moves.do_script: Teacher reviews and notes common themes.

output_product: An individual reflection naming one teaching move that supported critical thinking and one application to own learning.
contraindications: Do not use without prior modeling of metacognitive reflection.
Ensure the prompt is accessible to all students.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher displays a spectrum (e.g., left to right, progressive to conservative) and 2–3 media excerpts.
instructional_moves.say_script: Place each excerpt on the spectrum. Justify your placement with evidence from the text.
instructional_moves.do_script: Project the spectrum and excerpts. Assign pairs to place excerpts.

instructional_moves.description: Pairs place excerpts on the spectrum and justify.
instructional_moves.say_script: Use word choice, framing, and implied audience to justify your placement.
instructional_moves.do_script: Pairs write justifications on mini-whiteboards. Teacher circulates and names strong evidence.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher connects bias spectrum to the day's inquiry.
instructional_moves.say_script: Today we'll ask: how does bias construct different 'truths' about power?
instructional_moves.do_script: Record 2–3 strong justifications on the board and link to the EQ.

output_product: A pair-written placement of 2–3 media excerpts on a bias spectrum with evidence-based justifications.
contraindications: Do not use with highly polarizing current events without sensitivity protocols.
Ensure the spectrum is clearly defined and accessible.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher displays a short primary source or excerpt.
instructional_moves.say_script: What voices or perspectives are missing from this archive? Why might they be silenced?
instructional_moves.do_script: Project the excerpt. Give students 3 minutes to write.

instructional_moves.description: Students write their silence analysis.
instructional_moves.say_script: Name at least one silenced voice and one possible reason for the silence.
instructional_moves.do_script: Students write. Teacher collects responses.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher connects silences to the day's inquiry.
instructional_moves.say_script: Today we'll ask: how do silences construct power and knowledge?
instructional_moves.do_script: Read 1–2 strong responses aloud and link to the EQ.

output_product: An individual quickwrite naming at least one silenced voice and one possible reason for the silence.
contraindications: Do not use with excerpts that are too complex for a 7-minute warm-up.
Ensure students have prior exposure to archive silence concepts.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher introduces critical race counter-framing as challenging dominant racial narratives.
instructional_moves.say_script: We'll use a critical race lens to identify and challenge dominant racial narratives in this text.
instructional_moves.do_script: Display a simple definition and 1–2 examples.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher models identifying a dominant racial narrative and counter-framing it.
instructional_moves.say_script: This passage constructs ______ as ______. A counter-frame might center ______ instead.
instructional_moves.do_script: Annotate the excerpt, marking the dominant narrative and counter-frame.

instructional_moves.description: Students identify and counter-frame a dominant racial narrative in a new excerpt.
instructional_moves.say_script: Find one dominant racial narrative. Write a counter-frame that centers a marginalized perspective.
instructional_moves.do_script: Students write individually or in pairs. Teacher collects examples for discussion.

output_product: A written analysis identifying one dominant racial narrative and a counter-frame that centers a marginalized perspective.
contraindications: Do not use without prior instruction on critical race concepts.
Ensure a safe classroom culture for discussing race.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher introduces hegemony and manufactured consent in accessible language.
instructional_moves.say_script: Hegemony is how dominant groups maintain power through consent rather than force. We'll look for how this text manufactures consent.
instructional_moves.do_script: Display a simple definition and 1–2 examples.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher models identifying manufactured consent in a short text.
instructional_moves.say_script: Notice how this phrase positions ______ as natural or inevitable. What alternatives are left out?
instructional_moves.do_script: Annotate the excerpt, marking manufactured consent moves.

instructional_moves.description: Students identify one manufactured consent move in a new excerpt.
instructional_moves.say_script: Find one phrase that manufactures consent. Write: What ideology is implied? What alternative is silenced?
instructional_moves.do_script: Students write individually or in pairs. Teacher collects examples for discussion.

output_product: A written analysis identifying one manufactured consent move, the implied ideology, and one silenced alternative.
contraindications: Do not use with texts where hegemony is too subtle for students' current level.
Ensure students have prior exposure to basic hegemony concepts.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher introduces decolonial mapping as re-centering indigenous and marginalized geographies.
instructional_moves.say_script: We'll map how colonial power constructs space and how decolonial perspectives re-center marginalized geographies.
instructional_moves.do_script: Display a colonial map and a decolonial counter-map.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher models comparing colonial and decolonial maps.
instructional_moves.say_script: Notice how the colonial map centers ______. The decolonial map re-centers ______.
instructional_moves.do_script: Annotate both maps, highlighting key contrasts.

instructional_moves.description: Students compare colonial and decolonial maps in pairs.
instructional_moves.say_script: Find one contrast. Write: How does this change your understanding of power and space?
instructional_moves.do_script: Pairs write on mini-whiteboards. Teacher circulates and names strong comparisons.

output_product: A pair-written comparison of colonial and decolonial maps noting one contrast and how it changes understanding of power and space.
contraindications: Do not use without access to both colonial and decolonial maps.
Ensure students have prior exposure to basic colonial/decolonial concepts.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher introduces code-switching as a rhetorical strategy.
instructional_moves.say_script: Code-switching is when speakers shift language or style to navigate different audiences. We'll analyze how this constructs power.
instructional_moves.do_script: Display a simple definition and 1–2 examples.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher models identifying code-switching in a short text.
instructional_moves.say_script: Notice how the speaker shifts from ______ to ______. This positions different audiences to ______.
instructional_moves.do_script: Annotate the excerpt, marking code-switching moves.

instructional_moves.description: Students identify one code-switching move in a new excerpt.
instructional_moves.say_script: Find one code-switch. Write: What audiences are addressed? How does this construct power?
instructional_moves.do_script: Students write individually or in pairs. Teacher collects examples for discussion.

output_product: A written analysis identifying one code-switching move, the audiences addressed, and how this constructs power.
contraindications: Do not use with texts that lack clear code-switching.
Ensure students have prior exposure to basic code-switching concepts.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher introduces structural irony as a gap between appearance and reality at the text's level.
instructional_moves.say_script: Structural irony is when the text's overall structure creates a gap between what seems true and what is true. We'll decode this.
instructional_moves.do_script: Display a simple definition and 1–2 examples.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher models identifying structural irony in a short text.
instructional_moves.say_script: On the surface, this text seems to say ______. But the structure suggests ______.
instructional_moves.do_script: Annotate the excerpt, marking ironic gaps.

instructional_moves.description: Students identify one structural irony in a new excerpt.
instructional_moves.say_script: Find one ironic gap. Write: What seems true vs. what is true? What power dynamic does this reveal?
instructional_moves.do_script: Students write individually or in pairs. Teacher collects examples for discussion.

output_product: A written analysis identifying one structural irony, the gap between appearance and reality, and what power dynamic this reveals.
contraindications: Do not use with texts that lack clear structural irony.
Ensure students have prior exposure to basic irony concepts.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher introduces intersectionality as analyzing how multiple identities intersect to shape power.
instructional_moves.say_script: We'll use an intersectional matrix to analyze how race, gender, class, and other identities intersect in this text.
instructional_moves.do_script: Display a simple matrix template with identities as rows and power dynamics as columns.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher models filling in one cell of the matrix.
instructional_moves.say_script: For this character, race and gender intersect to produce ______. Notice how this differs from ______.
instructional_moves.do_script: Annotate the matrix on the board, filling in one cell with textual evidence.

instructional_moves.description: Students fill in one cell of the matrix in pairs.
instructional_moves.say_script: Choose one character or group. Fill in one cell with evidence. How does this intersection shape power?
instructional_moves.do_script: Pairs write on mini-whiteboards. Teacher circulates and names strong intersections.

output_product: A pair-written intersectional matrix cell analyzing how multiple identities intersect to shape power, supported by textual evidence.
contraindications: Do not use with texts that lack clear intersectional dynamics.
Ensure students have prior exposure to basic intersectionality concepts.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher sets up multiple 'café tables' each with a different critical question or text.
instructional_moves.say_script: Rotate through cafés. At each, discuss the question and record key insights.
instructional_moves.do_script: Display questions at each table. Assign starting tables.

instructional_moves.description: Groups rotate and discuss each question.
instructional_moves.say_script: Spend 8 minutes per table. Build on previous groups' notes.
instructional_moves.do_script: Groups rotate and discuss. Teacher circulates and names strong connections.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher leads a whole-class synthesis of café insights.
instructional_moves.say_script: What patterns emerged across cafés? How do these connect to our EQ?
instructional_moves.do_script: Facilitate a whole-class discussion. Record key insights on the board.

output_product: Rotational discussion notes at multiple café tables, plus a whole-class synthesis connecting patterns to the EQ.
contraindications: Do not use with too many cafés; limit to 4–5 for a 35-minute activity.
Ensure all questions are accessible enough for sustained discussion.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher labels four corners with ideological positions (e.g., strongly agree, agree, disagree, strongly disagree).
instructional_moves.say_script: Move to the corner that best represents your position on this statement: [debatable statement].
instructional_moves.do_script: Display the statement. Label corners.

instructional_moves.description: Students discuss their position in corners, then debate across corners.
instructional_moves.say_script: In your corner, prepare one argument. Then share across corners.
instructional_moves.do_script: Students discuss in corners, then debate. Teacher facilitates.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher leads a reflection on how positions shifted.
instructional_moves.say_script: Did anyone change corners? What evidence or argument shifted your thinking?
instructional_moves.do_script: Facilitate a whole-class reflection. Record key insights on the board.

output_product: A whole-class debate with tracked argument moves and a reflection on position shifts.
contraindications: Do not use with highly sensitive topics without established norms and safeguards.
Ensure the debatable statement is clear and accessible.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher forms triads and assigns each member a critical lens (e.g., historical, feminist, Marxist).
instructional_moves.say_script: Each person will critique the text from your assigned lens. Use evidence.
instructional_moves.do_script: Assign lenses and distribute lens guiding questions.

instructional_moves.description: Triads critique a text or student draft using their lenses.
instructional_moves.say_script: Share your lens-based critique. Then synthesize: what does each lens reveal?
instructional_moves.do_script: Students discuss and record critiques. Teacher circulates and names strong syntheses.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher leads a whole-class share-out of triad insights.
instructional_moves.say_script: Share one insight from your triad. How did multiple lenses deepen your analysis?
instructional_moves.do_script: Call on 2–3 triads to share. Record key insights on the board.

output_product: A triad-written critique of a text or draft from multiple critical lenses, plus a synthesis of insights.
contraindications: Do not use without prior instruction on critical lenses.
Ensure all lenses are clearly defined and accessible.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher introduces affinity mapping as grouping similar ideas or themes.
instructional_moves.say_script: Read these counter-stories. Then group similar themes or ideas together.
instructional_moves.do_script: Distribute counter-story excerpts and sticky notes.

instructional_moves.description: Groups read counter-stories and create affinity maps.
instructional_moves.say_script: Write one theme per sticky note. Group similar themes. Label each group.
instructional_moves.do_script: Groups create affinity maps on VNPS or large paper. Teacher circulates and names strong groupings.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher leads a gallery walk and names patterns.
instructional_moves.say_script: Notice which themes recur. How do these counter-stories challenge dominant narratives?
instructional_moves.do_script: Students walk and observe. Teacher highlights 2–3 strong maps.

output_product: A group-created affinity map of counter-story themes, with labeled groups and recurring patterns.
contraindications: Do not use with too many counter-stories; limit to 3–4 for a 30-minute activity.
Ensure all counter-stories are accessible enough for quick analysis.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher introduces the manifesto task.
instructional_moves.say_script: Write a manifesto that challenges a dominant discourse and proposes an alternative.
instructional_moves.do_script: Display the task and success criteria.

instructional_moves.description: Students draft their manifesto.
instructional_moves.say_script: Aim for 1–2 pages. Use rhetorical strategies. Clearly state the dominant discourse and your alternative.
instructional_moves.do_script: Students write. Teacher conferences with individuals as needed.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher provides formative feedback on drafts.
instructional_moves.say_script: I'll confer with each of you. Focus on how clearly your manifesto challenges the dominant discourse.
instructional_moves.do_script: Teacher holds brief conferences. Students revise as time allows.

output_product: A 1–2 page manifesto draft challenging a dominant discourse and proposing an alternative.
contraindications: Do not use without prior analysis of dominant discourses.
Ensure students have access to writing supports (frames, examples).

instructional_moves.description: Teacher introduces the policy rewrite task.
instructional_moves.say_script: Rewrite a policy or law to better serve marginalized communities.
instructional_moves.do_script: Display the task and success criteria.

instructional_moves.description: Students draft their policy rewrite.
instructional_moves.say_script: Aim for 1–2 pages. Use specific language. Explain how your rewrite addresses inequities.
instructional_moves.do_script: Students write. Teacher conferences with individuals as needed.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher provides formative feedback on drafts.
instructional_moves.say_script: I'll confer with each of you. Focus on how clearly your rewrite addresses inequities.
instructional_moves.do_script: Teacher holds brief conferences. Students revise as time allows.

output_product: A 1–2 page policy rewrite draft addressing inequities and better serving marginalized communities.
contraindications: Do not use without prior analysis of the original policy.
Ensure students have access to writing supports (frames, examples).

instructional_moves.description: Teacher introduces the archival counter-dossier task.
instructional_moves.say_script: Compile a dossier of 3–5 primary sources that challenge a dominant historical narrative.
instructional_moves.do_script: Display the task and success criteria.

instructional_moves.description: Students select and annotate primary sources for their dossier.
instructional_moves.say_script: For each source, write a brief annotation: source, claim, evidence, and how it challenges the dominant narrative.
instructional_moves.do_script: Students research and annotate. Teacher confers as needed.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher provides formative feedback on dossiers.
instructional_moves.say_script: I'll review your dossiers. Focus on how well your sources challenge the dominant narrative.
instructional_moves.do_script: Teacher reviews and provides written or verbal feedback.

output_product: An archival counter-dossier of 3–5 annotated primary sources challenging a dominant historical narrative.
contraindications: Do not use without prior instruction on source evaluation.
Ensure students have access to research tools and databases.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher introduces the podcast scripting task.
instructional_moves.say_script: Write a script for a short podcast episode that tells a counter-narrative.
instructional_moves.do_script: Display the task and success criteria.

instructional_moves.description: Students draft their podcast script.
instructional_moves.say_script: Aim for 3–5 minutes when read aloud. Use dialogue, sound cues, and narration.
instructional_moves.do_script: Students write. Teacher conferences with individuals as needed.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher provides formative feedback on scripts.
instructional_moves.say_script: I'll confer with each of you. Focus on how clearly your script tells a counter-narrative.
instructional_moves.do_script: Teacher holds brief conferences. Students revise as time allows.

output_product: A 3–5 minute podcast script draft telling a counter-narrative, with dialogue, sound cues, and narration.
contraindications: Do not use without prior analysis of counter-narratives.
Ensure students have access to writing supports (frames, examples).

instructional_moves.description: Teacher introduces the 3-2-1 slip format.
instructional_moves.say_script: Write: 3 things you learned, 2 questions you still have, 1 connection to our unit question.
instructional_moves.do_script: Display the prompt. Distribute slips or digital form.

instructional_moves.description: Students complete their 3-2-1 slip.
instructional_moves.say_script: Be specific. Use textual references where possible.
instructional_moves.do_script: Students write. Teacher collects responses.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher reviews slips to inform the next lesson.
instructional_moves.say_script: I'll read these to plan our next steps. Notice any patterns or misconceptions.
instructional_moves.do_script: Teacher reviews and notes common themes.

output_product: An individual 3-2-1 slip noting 3 things learned, 2 questions, and 1 connection to the unit question.
contraindications: Do not use with overly broad prompts; keep the question focused.
Ensure the prompt is accessible to all students.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher introduces the liberatory action commitment prompt.
instructional_moves.say_script: What is one action you can take, however small, to apply today's learning in the world?
instructional_moves.do_script: Display the prompt. Distribute slips or digital form.

instructional_moves.description: Students write their action commitment.
instructional_moves.say_script: Be specific. Name the action, audience, and timeline.
instructional_moves.do_script: Students write. Teacher collects responses.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher reviews commitments to track action orientation.
instructional_moves.say_script: I'll read these to see how you're applying learning. Notice any patterns.
instructional_moves.do_script: Teacher reviews and notes common themes.

output_product: An individual action commitment naming one specific action, audience, and timeline.
contraindications: Do not use without prior discussion of feasible actions.
Ensure the prompt is accessible to all students.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher forms visibly random groups of 3 and assigns each group a vertical non-permanent surface.
instructional_moves.say_script: You'll be working in randomly assigned groups of three at the boards. Your task is to build a 'forensic board' that shows how this text constructs power and meaning.
instructional_moves.do_script: Use a randomizer to assign students to groups of 3. Direct each group to a different vertical surface. Display the focus question and text excerpt.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher models the five board sections using a short sample excerpt.
instructional_moves.say_script: Your board will have five sections: Evidence, Inference, Root Cause, Complication, and Question/Action. Watch how I model this with a short excerpt.
instructional_moves.do_script: On a central board, draw five labeled sections. With a sample excerpt, write one piece of textual evidence, one inference, one systemic root cause, one complication, and one question or action.

instructional_moves.description: Groups read the assigned excerpt and populate all five sections on their VNPS.
instructional_moves.say_script: In your groups, read the excerpt. Then fill all five sections: Evidence (what the text says), Inference (what it suggests), Root Cause (systemic or institutional source), Complication (counter-evidence or limit), and Question/Action (what we still need to know or could do).
instructional_moves.do_script: Students annotate the text individually for 2 minutes, then collaboratively write on the board. Teacher circulates, asking probing questions and naming strong moves.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher leads a brief gallery walk and highlights patterns and tensions across boards.
instructional_moves.say_script: We'll do a quick gallery walk. Notice where boards agree, where they diverge, and where a complication forced a revision of an inference.
instructional_moves.do_script: Students step away from their boards and walk silently for 2 minutes. Teacher names 2–3 specific observations about reasoning, not just content.

output_product: A completed VNPS 'forensic board' with five labeled sections (Evidence, Inference, Root Cause, Complication, Question/Action) that uses at least two direct textual references and names one systemic or institutional factor.
contraindications: Do not use when the learning target is basic recall or plot summary without interpretation.
Do not use if vertical surfaces are unavailable and no equivalent visible collaborative space can be created.
If groups are larger than 4, split them; larger groups reduce individual accountability on VNPS.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher models Turn 1: provisional claim + strongest evidence.
instructional_moves.say_script: I'm entering this text with the assumption that ______. The strongest evidence I see so far is ______, which suggests ______.
instructional_moves.do_script: Display the excerpt/data on the board. Underline or annotate the specific phrase or data point that supports the provisional claim. Label this 'Turn 1: Provisional Claim'.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher models Turn 2: counter-evidence or counter-reading.
instructional_moves.say_script: A rigorous counterclaim or alternative reading posits that ______. Here's the evidence that complicates my first claim: ______.
instructional_moves.do_script: Annotate a second passage or data point that contradicts or complicates Turn 1. Label this 'Turn 2: Counter-Evidence / Counter-Reading'.

instructional_moves.description: Teacher models Turn 3: revised claim + ethical/epistemic limit.
instructional_moves.say_script: I am revising my initial claim because ______. A more defensible claim is ______. The ethical or epistemic limit of this claim is ______.
instructional_moves.do_script: Write the revised claim next to Turns 1 and 2. Add a brief note naming the ethical or epistemic limit. Label this 'Turn 3: Revised Claim + Limit'.

instructional_moves.description: Students rehearse the 3-turn structure in pairs using a different excerpt.
instructional_moves.say_script: In pairs, use the same 3-turn structure with this new excerpt. Turn 1: provisional claim + evidence. Turn 2: counter-evidence or counter-reading. Turn 3: revised claim + limit.
instructional_moves.do_script: Students annotate a second excerpt on mini-whiteboards or paper, drafting their own 3-turn sequence. Teacher circulates and names strong examples of revision.

output_product: A visible 3-turn claim revision sequence (provisional claim → counter-evidence/reading → revised claim + ethical/epistemic limit) on VNPS, mini-whiteboard, or annotation sheet, using at least one textual or data reference per turn.
contraindications: Do not use when the lesson's primary target is basic comprehension or plot recall without interpretation.
Do not use if the text set lacks sufficient complexity or tension to support a genuine counter-reading.
Do not compress into fewer than three distinct turns; if time is tight, shorten excerpts, not the reasoning.
